title: 09. Evaluation: Multi-Agent System Evaluation: Coordination, Communication, and Emergent Behavior
summary: A single agent is one LLM making one decision per step. A multi-agent system (MAS) is N agents, each making decisions, plus a coordination layer that decides who speaks next, who sees what, and when to stop.
objectives: Why Multi-Agent Eval is Harder Than Single-Agent

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
> **Prerequisite**: File 04 (single-agent eval). You understand trajectories, tool-use metrics, and the agent loop.
>
> **Scope**: Systems where *more than one* LLM agent collaborates, debates, or hands off work — AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph multi-node, custom orchestrators. We assume each individual agent already has the file-04 metrics.

sections.title: 1. Why Multi-Agent Eval is Harder Than Single-Agent
sections.body:
A single agent is one LLM making one decision per step. A **multi-agent system** (MAS) is *N* agents, each making decisions, *plus* a coordination layer that decides who speaks next, who sees what, and when to stop. The state space explodes.

Three structural problems make MAS eval qualitatively harder:

1. **Composition explosion.** A single agent has a trajectory of length *S* with *T* tools. A multi-agent system with *N* agents has on the order of *N × S × M* messages, where *M* is the number of message types (broadcast, point-to-point, handoff, vote). The number of possible trajectories grows combinatorially with agent count. You cannot enumerate them; you can only sample.
2. **Communication overhead.** Agents spend tokens talking *to each other*, not to the user. A 3-agent debate can burn 10× the tokens of a single agent for the same final answer. Token cost is no longer a clean proxy for "work done on the task".
3. **Emergent behavior.** Behaviors appear at the team level that no single agent exhibits: echo chambers, spontaneous division of labor, sycophantic agreement, infinite "I agree with you" loops. These are properties of the *interaction*, not any one agent.

On top of all this sits the **credit assignment problem**: when the final answer is wrong, which agent failed? Was it the researcher that retrieved bad evidence, the critic that failed to challenge it, or the summarizer that dropped a key fact? Single-agent eval has one throat to choke. Multi-agent eval has *N* suspects and a conspiracy.

```
   SINGLE-AGENT                         MULTI-AGENT (N=3)
   ============                         =================

   task ──▶ [AGENT] ──▶ answer          task ──▶ ┌────────┐
                                                │ AGENT A│─┐
   one trajectory                               └────────┘ │
   one failure point                                     ▼
   easy to attribute                           ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
                                              │AGENT B │◀▶│AGENT C │
                                              └────────┘  └────────┘
                                                   │           │
                                                   ▼           ▼
                                                ??? answer ??? (and whose fault?)
```

The left side has one arrow and one box. The right side has agents, channels, handoffs, contention, and an ambiguous output. Every additional arrow is a new failure mode and a new attribution question.

sections.title: 2. Multi-Agent Architectures (Quick Overview)
sections.body:
Different architectures fail differently. Pick metrics that match the topology.

### 2.1 Sequential Pipeline

```
   task ──▶ [A:research] ──▶ [B:analyze] ──▶ [C:write] ──▶ answer
```

Each agent consumes the previous agent's output. Simplest to attribute: errors propagate forward. **Information loss** at handoffs is the dominant failure mode.

### 2.2 Hierarchical (Manager + Workers)

```
                        ┌──▶ [Worker 1] ──┐
   task ──▶ [Manager] ──┼──▶ [Worker 2] ──┼──▶ [Manager] ──▶ answer
                        └──▶ [Worker 3] ──┘
```

The manager delegates, collects, integrates. Key risks: manager becomes a **bottleneck**; workers under-utilized; manager over-rules correct workers.

### 2.3 Peer-to-Peer / Debate

```
            ┌─────────────── loop ───────────────┐
            ▼                                    │
        [Agent A] ◀──argue──▶ [Agent B] ◀──argree─▶ [Agent C]
            │                                    │
            └──────────▶ consensus? ──yes────────┘
                                  │
                                  ▼
                              answer
```

Agents criticize each other until they converge (or hit a round cap). Failure modes: **echo chambers**, never-converging debates, premature consensus.

### 2.4 Round-Robin / Competitive

```
   task ──▶ [A] ──▶ [B] ──▶ [C] ──▶ [A] ──▶ [B] ──▶ ... ──▶ [judge] ──▶ answer
```

Each agent takes a turn refining the artifact; a judge (sometimes external, sometimes a designated agent) picks the best. Failure modes: later agents coast on earlier work; the judge is biased toward the last speaker.

The architecture determines which metrics matter most. Pipelines care about **information loss**; hierarchies care about **role effectiveness**; debates care about **convergence speed** and **conflict resolution**.

sections.title: 3. Core Multi-Agent Metrics
sections.body:
Each metric targets a failure mode that single-agent metrics miss.

### 3.1 Task Success Rate (TSR)

**Definition**: Same as single-agent — fraction of tasks the system completes correctly. Binary or graded.

**Intuition**: Still the only metric the user cares about. The others diagnose *why* TSR is what it is.

**When to use**: Always, as the headline number.

### 3.2 Coordination Efficiency

**Definition**: Fraction of inter-agent messages that *advance the task* versus redundant, repeated, or no-op messages.

**Formula**: `useful_messages / total_messages`. A message is "useful" if it introduces new information, a decision, or a handoff; "redundant" if it restates prior content or is a pure acknowledgment (`"I agree."`, `"Good point."`).

**When to use**: Any architecture with peer-to-peer chatter. A system with TSR=0.9 but coordination efficiency=0.2 is wasting 80% of its tokens on social pleasantries.

### 3.3 Communication Overhead

**Definition**: Tokens spent on inter-agent communication divided by total tokens consumed.

**Formula**: `inter_agent_tokens / (inter_agent_tokens + task_tokens)`. Task tokens are those spent on tool calls, retrieval, and the final answer.

**When to use**: Cost-sensitive deployments. A debate system that spends 70% of tokens on agents agreeing with each other is structurally inefficient.

### 3.4 Role Effectiveness

**Definition**: Per-agent score for whether the agent did its assigned job. For a "researcher" agent: did it retrieve evidence? For a "critic": did it raise at least one substantive objection?

**Formula**: `LLM-as-judge(role_description, agent_messages) -> score in [0,1]` averaged across agents.

**When to use**: Any system with predefined roles (CrewAI, role-tagged AutoGen). Catches the failure mode where a "critic" agent silently degrades into a yes-man.

### 3.5 Conflict Resolution Success

**Definition**: When agents disagree, did the system pick the *correct* resolution? Requires ground truth on the disputed point.

**Formula**: `correct_resolutions / total_disputes`. A "dispute" is any turn where one agent explicitly contradicts another.

**When to use**: Debate and hierarchical systems. A system that surfaces disputes but resolves them wrong is worse than one that never disputes at all — it looks rigorous while being broken.

### 3.6 Convergence Speed

**Definition**: For debate/consensus systems, the number of rounds until agents stop changing their positions (or until they agree).

**Formula**: `rounds_to_convergence / max_allowed_rounds`. Lower is better.

**When to use**: Debate architectures. Non-convergence is a hard failure (system hits the round cap with no consensus).

### 3.7 Information Loss

**Definition**: Fraction of task-relevant information present in agent *i*'s output that survives into agent *i+1*'s input.

**Formula**: `shared_key_facts(i, i+1) / key_facts_in(i)`. Key facts are extracted by an LLM or by ground-truth annotation.

**When to use**: Sequential pipelines and hierarchical handoffs. Silent information loss is the most common pipeline failure.

### 3.8 Cascading Error Rate

**Definition**: Probability that an error in agent *i* propagates to an error in the final answer, given that downstream agents had a chance to catch it.

**Formula**: `final_errors_caused_by_agent_i / errors_made_by_agent_i`.

**When to use**: Diagnosing robustness. A high cascade rate means downstream agents are not correcting upstream mistakes; a low cascade rate means the system self-heals.

### 3.9 Specialization Score

**Definition**: How distinct is each agent's behavior from the others? Measured via overlap of tool usage, vocabulary, or action distribution.

**Formula**: `1 - pairwise_behavioral_overlap`. Overlap is e.g. Jaccard similarity of tool-call sets per agent pair, averaged.

**When to use**: Any system where roles are supposed to differ. Low specialization means you are paying for N agents but getting 1 worth of behavior — a single agent would do.

### Comparison Table

| Metric | What it catches | Architecture fit | Cost to compute |
|---|---|---|---|
| Task Success Rate | Final answer wrong | All | Low (ground truth) |
| Coordination Efficiency | Wasted chatter | Peer-to-peer, debate | Medium (judge) |
| Communication Overhead | Token blowup from talking | All multi-agent | Low (token counting) |
| Role Effectiveness | Agent not doing its job | Role-based (CrewAI) | Medium (judge per agent) |
| Conflict Resolution Success | Disputes resolved wrong | Debate, hierarchical | High (needs ground truth on disputes) |
| Convergence Speed | Non-terminating debates | Debate | Low (round counting) |
| Information Loss | Silent handoff dropouts | Sequential pipeline | High (key-fact extraction) |
| Cascading Error Rate | Upstream errors flow through | All | High (per-error tracing) |
| Specialization Score | Agents duplicating work | All | Medium (behavioral overlap) |

sections.title: 5. Framework-Specific Eval Patterns
sections.body:
The big three frameworks expose different instrumentation surfaces.

### AutoGen

AutoGen's primary abstraction is the **conversation graph**: agents send messages to each other in patterns you define (GroupChat, sequential chat, nested chat). Eval surfaces:

- **Conversation transcript** is your trajectory. Parse it into `(sender, receiver, content, round)` tuples.
- **Role adherence**: each agent has a system prompt; judge whether its messages stay in role.
- **Speaker selection**: AutoGen's GroupChat picks the next speaker. Evaluate whether the *right* agent spoke at each turn. A researcher answering a code question is a role violation.
- **Termination**: AutoGen terminates on a keyword or round cap. Log whether termination was *natural* (agent said "TERMINATE") or *forced* (hit cap). High forced-termination rates signal non-convergence.

### CrewAI

CrewAI's primary abstraction is the **crew**: a set of agents with roles, a set of tasks assigned to agents, and a process (sequential or hierarchical). Eval surfaces:

- **Task-to-agent fit**: was each task assigned to the agent whose role best matches? CrewAI lets you pin tasks to agents; measure whether dynamic assignment (when used) picks correctly.
- **Crew-level success**: did the *crew* complete its overall goal, regardless of individual task success?
- **Per-task output quality**: each task produces an artifact; score each one against its task description.
- **Handoff artifacts**: CrewAI passes task outputs as context to the next task. Measure **information loss** at each handoff.

### LangGraph Multi-Node

LangGraph's primary abstraction is the **state graph**: nodes (agents or functions) connected by edges, with a shared state object. Eval surfaces:

- **State transitions**: every node reads/writes a typed state. Diff the state before and after each node to see exactly what each agent changed.
- **Node-level metrics**: treat each node like a single agent — compute TSR, tool accuracy, etc. per node.
- **Edge traversal**: which edges fired? Did the graph take the expected path? Unexpected edges (e.g., a "retry" edge firing 5 times) are red flags.
- **Cycle detection**: LangGraph permits cycles. Log how many times each cycle was traversed; cycles > 1 are often bugs.

| Framework | Trajectory unit | Role model | Topology | Key extra metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AutoGen | Message in conversation | System prompt per agent | Conversation graph | Speaker selection accuracy |
| CrewAI | Task output artifact | Role + goal per agent | Sequential or hierarchical | Task-to-agent fit |
| LangGraph | State diff per node | Implicit (node = role) | Arbitrary state graph | Edge traversal correctness |

sections.title: 6. Emergent Behavior Evaluation
sections.body:
**Emergent behavior** is behavior of the team that no single agent exhibits in isolation. It can be the whole point of multi-agent (creative division of labor) or the whole problem (echo chambers).

**Positive emergence**:

- *Spontaneous specialization* — agents gravitate toward different sub-tasks without explicit role assignment.
- *Creative synthesis* — debate produces an answer neither agent would have produced alone.
- *Mutual correction* — agent B catches agent A's error and the final answer is correct.

**Negative emergence**:

- *Echo chamber* — agents reinforce each other's wrong answer until it becomes confident-and-wrong.
- *Sycophancy* — agents agree with the most recent speaker to avoid conflict.
- *Infinite agreement loop* — agents ping-pong "I agree", "Yes, agreed", "Completely agree", burning rounds with no progress.
- *Role collapse* — a critic agent stops criticizing and starts summarizing; two agents converge to the same behavior.

### Detection

- **Trajectory analysis**: plot per-round token novelty (fraction of tokens not seen in prior rounds). A flat line means no new information is being introduced — a signature of loops.
- **Message pattern mining**: cluster messages by content. A cluster with 10 near-duplicate messages is an agreement loop.
- **Sentiment trajectory**: track agreement sentiment over rounds. A monotonically increasing sentiment curve that converges to "fully agree" before the task is solved is sycophancy.

### Code: Detecting Conversation Loops

```python
def detect_loop(messages, window=4, dup_threshold=3):
    """Flag a conversation window as a loop if `dup_threshold`
    of the last `window` messages are near-duplicates."""
    if len(messages) < window:
        return False
    recent = messages[-window:]
    # Tokenize and bag-of-words normalize
    bows = [frozenset(m.lower().split()) for m in recent]
    # Count pairwise near-duplicates (Jaccard > 0.7)
    dups = 0
    for i in range(len(bows)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(bows)):
            inter = len(bows[i] & bows[j])
            union = len(bows[i] | bows[j]) or 1
            if inter / union > 0.7:
                dups += 1
    return dups >= dup_threshold

# Example: a debate that devolves into agreement
msgs = [
    "The capital of France is Paris.",
    "Yes, the capital of France is Paris.",
    "Agreed, the capital of France is Paris.",
    "Correct, the capital of France is Paris.",
    "Right, the capital of France is Paris.",
]
print("Loop detected:", detect_loop(msgs))  # True
```

sections.title: 7. LLM-as-Judge for Multi-Agent
sections.body:
A single LLM-as-judge call on the final answer misses everything that makes multi-agent multi-agent. You need a **multi-criteria rubric** applied to the *full trajectory*.

### Multi-Criteria Rubric

| Criterion | Question | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Is the final answer correct? | 0.40 |
| Coordination | Did agents communicate efficiently, without redundancy? | 0.20 |
| Role adherence | Did each agent stay in role? | 0.15 |
| Conflict handling | Were disputes raised and resolved correctly? | 0.15 |
| Efficiency | Were tokens and rounds spent proportionally to difficulty? | 0.10 |

Weights are illustrative; tune per use case. The judge sees the entire transcript and scores each criterion on a 0–5 scale.

### Pairwise Comparison: Multi-Agent vs Single-Agent

The cleanest A/B for a multi-agent system is: take the same task, run a strong single-agent baseline, run the multi-agent system, and have a judge pick the better answer *blind* (judge does not know which is which). If multi-agent wins less than 60% of tasks, the architecture is not paying for itself.

### Cost Considerations

Judging a 10-agent trajectory is expensive: the judge must read every message. Approximate judge costs scale as `O(N × S)` in tokens — the same as the system itself. Mitigations:

- **Summarize-then-judge**: first LLM compresses the transcript to key decisions; judge scores the summary.
- **Per-agent judges**: one small judge per agent scores role adherence; a final judge scores the whole.
- **Sample, don't census**: judge 10% of trajectories in production, 100% in eval.

### Code: `judge_multi_agent_run()`

```python
def judge_multi_agent_run(transcript, task, rubric):
    """transcript: list of {agent, message, round}
       task: the original task string
       rubric: list of (criterion, weight, question)
       returns: composite score in [0,1] + per-criterion scores"""
    scores = {}
    for criterion, weight, question in rubric:
        prompt = f"""Task: {task}
        Transcript: {transcript}
        Question: {question}
        Score 0-5 (integer):"""
        raw = llm_call(prompt)  # returns e.g. "4"
        scores[criterion] = int(raw.strip()) / 5.0
    composite = sum(scores[c] * w for c, w, _ in rubric)
    return composite, scores
```

The dashboard's job is to make the credit assignment problem *visible*. The left pane tells you *who* is underperforming; the middle tells you *how* agents talked; the right tells you *why* the final answer came out wrong.

sections.title: 9. Code Example
sections.body:
Save as `multi_agent_eval.py`. Simulates a 3-agent debate (researcher, critic, summarizer), scores on task success, communication overhead, convergence rounds, and final answer quality. Pure Python, no LLM calls.

```python
"""Multi-agent debate evaluator (mock). Scores a 3-agent debate system."""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Tuple

@dataclass
class Message:
    agent: str
    content: str
    round: int
    tokens: int

@dataclass
class DebateRun:
    task: str
    ground_truth: str
    messages: List[Message] = field(default_factory=list)
    final_answer: str = ""
    max_rounds: int = 5

# --- Mock a debate: researcher proposes, critic challenges, summarizer closes ---
def mock_debate() -> DebateRun:
    run = DebateRun(
        task="What is the boiling point of water in Denver?",
        ground_truth="approx 95C due to high altitude",
    )
    run.messages = [
        Message("researcher", "Water boils at 100C at sea level.", 1, 12),
        Message("critic", "Denver is at altitude; pressure is lower.", 1, 14),
        Message("researcher", "Agree, boiling point drops with altitude.", 2, 15),
        Message("critic", "Yes, agree, boiling point drops with altitude.", 2, 14),
        Message("summarizer", "I agree, boiling point drops with altitude.", 2, 13),
        Message("summarizer", "Final: approx 95C due to altitude in Denver.", 3, 10),
    ]
    run.final_answer = "approx 95C due to altitude in Denver"
    return run

# --- Scoring functions ---
def task_success(run: DebateRun) -> float:
    key_terms = set(run.ground_truth.lower().replace(".", "").split())
    ans_terms = set(run.final_answer.lower().replace(".", "").split())
    overlap = len(key_terms & ans_terms) / max(len(key_terms), 1)
    return float(overlap >= 0.6)

def communication_overhead(run: DebateRun) -> float:
    """Fraction of tokens that are redundant (near-duplicate of a prior msg)."""
    seen_bows = []
    redundant_tokens = 0
    for m in run.messages:
        bow = frozenset(m.content.lower().split())
        is_dup = any(
            len(bow & prev) / max(len(bow | prev), 1) > 0.7 for prev in seen_bows
        )
        if is_dup:
            redundant_tokens += m.tokens
        seen_bows.append(bow)
    total = sum(m.tokens for m in run.messages) or 1
    return redundant_tokens / total  # lower is better

def convergence_rounds(run: DebateRun) -> int:
    """Round at which the summarizer commits to a final answer."""
    for m in run.messages:
        if m.agent == "summarizer" and m.content.lower().startswith("final"):
            return m.round
    return run.max_rounds  # did not converge

def answer_quality(run: DebateRun) -> float:
    key = set(run.ground_truth.lower().replace(".", "").split())
    ans = set(run.final_answer.lower().replace(".", "").split())
    return len(key & ans) / max(len(key), 1)

def evaluate(run: DebateRun) -> Dict[str, float]:
    return {
        "task_success": task_success(run),
        "comm_overhead": round(communication_overhead(run), 3),
        "convergence_rounds": convergence_rounds(run),
        "answer_quality": round(answer_quality(run), 3),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run = mock_debate()
    scores = evaluate(run)
    print("Task:", run.task)
    print("Ground truth:", run.ground_truth)
    print("Final answer:", run.final_answer)
    for k, v in scores.items():
        print(f"  {k:22s}: {v}")
```

Run with `python multi_agent_eval.py`. Expected output shows `task_success=1.0`, `comm_overhead≈0.35` (the round-2 critic and summarizer messages are near-duplicates of the round-2 researcher), `convergence_rounds=3`, `answer_quality≈0.83`.

sections.title: 10. Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
- **Optimizing individual agents does not optimize the team.** Each agent scoring 0.9 on its own eval does not imply the team scores 0.9. Coordination overhead, role overlap, and emergent loops can drag team TSR below any individual agent's score. Always evaluate the *system*, not just its parts.
- **Ignoring communication cost.** A multi-agent system that hits TSR=0.95 but costs 8× the tokens of a single agent is rarely worth it in production. Track cost-per-correct-answer, not just TSR.
- **Treating agents as interchangeable.** They are not. Swapping a "researcher" and a "critic" destroys role effectiveness and usually TSR. Eval systems must respect role assignment, not just agent identity.
- **No ground truth for intermediate steps.** Without per-step ground truth, you cannot measure information loss, cascading error rate, or do forward tracing. Invest in intermediate ground truth even when it is expensive — it is the only way to do credit assignment.
- **Multi-agent loops with no termination criterion.** Debate and peer-to-peer systems can run forever. Always set a round cap, and log how often the cap is the *reason* for termination. High cap-hit rates mean the system is not converging.
- **Judging only the final answer.** A correct final answer reached through 40 redundant messages is a different system from one reached through 6 efficient messages. Judge the trajectory.
- **Confusing "more agents" with "better".** Doubling agent count doubles cost and roughly squares the credit-assignment search space. Add agents only when a measured failure mode justifies it.

options: Two systems can have TSR=0.9 with wildly different cost profiles, coordination quality, and robustness.
Convergence is well-judged by three signals: (1) convergence rounds is well below the cap; (2) the final answer is correct; (3) at least one substantive dispute was…
Emergent behavior is team-level behavior no individual agent exhibits: spontaneous specialization, echo chambers, sycophancy, infinite agreement loops.
A single agent has one trajectory; the error must have occurred somewhere on it.
quiz.explanation: A single agent has one trajectory; the error must have occurred somewhere on it. A multi-agent system has N trajectories plus a coordination layer, and the final answer is a function of all of them. The error could originate in any agent, propagate through several, or emerge from the interaction itself.

options: Convergence is well-judged by three signals: (1) convergence rounds is well below the cap; (2) the final answer is correct; (3) at least one substantive dispute was…
Coordination efficiency is the fraction of inter-agent messages that advance the task.

quiz.explanation: Coordination efficiency is the fraction of inter-agent messages that advance the task. A message is redundant if it restates prior content or is a pure acknowledgment. Below 0.5 means more than half the messages are wasted chatter; below 0.3 is a structural problem, not noise.

quiz.explanation: Forward tracing starts at the task and walks through the agent graph, tagging each artifact correct/incorrect; the first incorrect artifact is the origin. Backward tracing starts at the wrong final answer and walks back, asking which agent's output was the proximate cause. Forward is one-pass and identifies origin; backward is more precise about the proximate cause but may miss upstream origins.
